snippet.title: He found $500,000 but was not allowed to keep it!
snippet.description:
In 2006, contractor Bob Kitts discovered $182,000 hidden behind a bathroom wall in a Cleveland home. The find, including Depression-era $500 and $1,000 bills, was believed to be worth up to over half a million dollars because of the rarity of some of the bills. However, the subsequent dispute over the money has brought misfortune to those involved. Kitts and homeowner Amanda Reece, who offered a 10% finder's fee, clashed over its distribution. Kitts, invoking a legal doctrine called "treasure trove," sued for all the money. The saga attracted global attention, but Reece filed for bankruptcy after exhausting the funds, leaving her financially destitute.

As the legal battle unfolded, Probate Magistrate Charles Brown ruled that 86% of the money, marked "P. Dunne," belonged to the heirs of the home's original owner, Patrick Dunne. The remaining 14% was unmarked and initially claimed by Reece, but she renounced her claim. Consequently, Kitts received that portion, totaling $3,456.51, significantly less than Reece's original offer. The 21 heirs received just over a thousand dollars each, with some portions going to their attorney and those who facilitated the connection. Despite the global attention, the dispute concluded with minimal gains for all parties involved.

snippet.title: 250 Years Later: Why Everything You Learned About the American Revolution is Wrong
snippet.description:
Forget what you learned in school. Or from Hamilton. The American revolution was bigger and bloodier than you ever thought.

For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we bring you the undiscovered stories, heroes, and villains of the War for Independence. We traverse the Atlantic and plunge deep into the American West to discover a multi-front war that engulfed a diverse cast of characters – Indigenous people, enslaved Africans, American Loyalists, women of all social classes – and changed the face of world history.

snippet.title: He was awarded $1 Million by mistake!
snippet.description:
In 2013, Kevin Lewis experienced a stroke of luck and a significant mistake when he won $1 million from Horseshoe Casino Cincinnati in August through a loyalty program. The mix-up arose when it was discovered that there were two men named Kevin Lewis of the same age living in Cincinnati. Despite the error, the casino decided to let the mistakenly identified Kevin Lewis keep the money and awarded the intended recipient a separate prize. However, the fortunate turn of events took a dark twist for Lewis, who appeared a year later in Hamilton County Common Pleas Court before Judge Jerome Metz Jr.

In court, the mistaken Lewis expressed remorse for selling marijuana and engaging in recreational drug use. He pleaded guilty to drug possession and trafficking in marijuana to have two other charges dropped. Avoiding a potential 5 1/2-year prison sentence, Lewis, formerly employed in inventory control at the Hyatt hotel, disclosed that the $1 million prize had been depleted, much of it used to settle bills for others. His attorney, Alvertis Bishop Jr., explained that a 2012 left hip replacement left Lewis disabled and dependent on painkillers, ultimately leading him down a path of drug addiction. The judge ordered Lewis to serve probation, attain his high school equivalency degree, suspended his driver’s license for two years, and mandated him to undergo drug and alcohol testing.
